TIP 1: Auto loan APR bait-and-switch at Pier 7 Financial
CHANNEL: encrypted email
RECEIVED: 02 May 2026

I am writing about consumer lending practices at Pier 7 Financial, a regional consumer bank with about $18 billion in assets, headquartered in Phoenix. I work in the bank's internal compliance group as a senior analyst on the consumer lending side. I joined the bank in March 2023 and have been on the consumer compliance team for the entire period since.

The issue I am reporting is a systematic bait-and-switch on auto loan APRs in the bank's indirect lending channel. Customers receive a rate quote at the dealership based on a Pier 7 rate sheet. After the loan documents are signed and the customer drives off, a portion of these loans are re-priced upward at booking on the bank's side, with the closing documents reflecting the higher rate. The customer's signature is on a document that does not show the same rate that was quoted.

The mechanism, as I have been able to reconstruct it, was implemented by our former Director of Consumer Credit, Lyle Mendin. I personally attended the rate-setting meeting in November 2022 where Mendin presented the "rate floor adjustment" framework to the consumer credit committee, including how the system would re-price loans booked from a defined list of dealer partners. That framework went into production in early 2023 and has been running since.

Across 28 months I have identified 4,200 affected loans averaging $450 in additional interest charges per loan over the life of the loan, totaling approximately $2.1 million in customer overcharges. The bank is actively negotiating with two state attorneys general and has set aside approximately $2.7 million in reserves for the matter, which the consumer credit team has internally referred to as "the Mendin issue."

The mechanism is technically defensible to a casual auditor because the closed loan document does include the higher rate; the customer's signature is treated as legal consent. What the documentation does not show is the rate the customer was originally quoted at the dealership, which a parallel internal system records but which is not retained in the customer file.

I have:

- Copies of the November 2022 rate framework deck.
- Quarterly compliance reports for 2024 and 2025 showing the loan flagging logic.
- A spreadsheet I assembled cross-referencing original dealer-quoted rates against booked rates for 4,200 loans across 2024 and 2025.
- Email correspondence with our consumer compliance lead in early 2025 in which I raised this and was told the practice was "within the dealer disclosure framework."

I would prefer initial contact be with the CFPB or the relevant state attorney general rather than the bank. I am still employed at Pier 7 and am submitting this anonymously through a personal channel.

TIP 2: Customer data exposure through misconfigured cloud storage at Cordwain Logistics
CHANNEL: secure drop
RECEIVED: 06 May 2026

I work as a senior network engineer at Cordwain Logistics, a third-party logistics provider with about 9,000 employees and customers across the retail, healthcare, and consumer electronics sectors. I have been at Cordwain since 2021. I am reporting what I believe is an undisclosed customer data exposure event that the company has known about for at least seven months and has not notified affected parties about.

The exposure began in roughly mid-2024 when our cloud platform team migrated a portion of the customer-portal infrastructure to AWS S3-backed storage. One of the buckets — used for staging customer-uploaded shipment manifests, including manifests that contain product SKUs, recipient PHI for our healthcare logistics customers, and pricing terms for our retail customers — was deployed with public-read ACLs.

The bucket, named cw-cust-portal-staging-prd, was publicly accessible from approximately June 2024 through October 2025. During that 16-month window the bucket received approximately 14 terabytes of customer-uploaded files. Server access logs, which I was able to review in my role, show that the bucket was indexed by at least three known security-research crawlers in early 2025 and was accessed by at least 47 distinct IP addresses outside our corporate range across the period. The total number of files exposed was approximately 1.2 million, of which my sampling estimates that about 8 percent contained PHI subject to HIPAA notification requirements.

The exposure was identified by an external security researcher in October 2025 and reported to our CISO Rohan Bakshi via the bug bounty program. The bucket ACL was corrected within four hours of the report. What has not happened since then is customer notification.

I attended an internal review on 14 October 2025 chaired by our General Counsel Helena Aldemar, with Bakshi, our CFO, and the head of our healthcare logistics division. The discussion focused on whether the exposure constituted a "reportable breach" under the contractual terms with our healthcare customers and under HIPAA. The position taken by counsel was that, in the absence of evidence of "specific exfiltration of PHI by a known threat actor," the bank — sorry, the company — would not provide proactive notification.

I had read access during this period to the CFO's confidential exposure analysis prepared for the board, which estimated remediation and litigation reserves of $12 to $18 million in a notification scenario and $0 in a no-notification scenario. The choice not to notify is documented in writing in the 22 October 2025 board update package, which CISO Rohan Bashki signed alongside our General Counsel.

I have retained: the bucket configuration history, the access logs, my notes from the 14 October review, and a copy of the 22 October board package as Bakshi distributed it. I have not yet notified any external authority. My concern is for the patients whose information was exposed and who have not been told.

TIP 3: Controlled-substance diversion by CRNA at Belden Regional Health
CHANNEL: intake form
RECEIVED: 30 April 2026

I work as a forensic accountant in the internal audit department at Belden Regional Health, a five-hospital nonprofit health system based in central Indiana. I have been at Belden since 2019 and have specialized in pharmacy diversion investigations since 2022. I am writing about a pattern of controlled-substance diversion that I believe is being inadequately addressed by hospital leadership.

The subject of this tip is Vance Doroshow, a Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetist (CRNA) who has been employed at Belden's flagship hospital, Belden Regional Medical Center, since 2017. CRNAs at our hospital are advanced practice nurses with prescriptive authority for controlled substances used in anesthesia care. Throughout this tip I will refer to Doroshow as a CRNA where the role is relevant and as a "nurse" where I am referring to him generically as a hospital employee subject to the nursing professional code.

The pattern I have documented is a discrepancy between fentanyl and hydromorphone vial withdrawals from the OR-2 automated dispensing cabinet, attributed to Doroshow's logon, and corresponding documented administration in the anesthesia record. I conducted a reconciliation covering fiscal Q2 of 2025 — that is, the calendar quarter October through December 2024, on Belden's July-anchored fiscal year — and again across fiscal Q3 (January through March 2025).

In fiscal Q2 2025, my reconciliation identified 27 vials confirmed missing on inventory reconciliation against patient charting and waste documentation. By the time I completed my fiscal Q3 review and was able to add subsequently identified discrepancies that had not been confirmed at the time of the Q2 close, the total of suspected diverted vials across the Q2 period stood at 29 — the additional two were identified as suspected diversion during Q3 reconciliation but were originating from Q2 dispensings that had been closed in the interim.

I escalated to our Chief Pharmacy Officer in February 2025 and to our Chief Medical Officer in March 2025. A peer review committee was convened in April 2025 and concluded — without interviewing Doroshow — that the discrepancies were attributable to "documentation timing variance." Doroshow has continued to practice. He has not been referred to the State Board of Nursing or to the DEA. The hospital's general counsel, in a written opinion dated 28 April 2025 that I have seen, recommended against external referral on the grounds that the documentation was "ambiguous as to specific intent."

My concern is twofold. First, that diversion at this volume is consistent with the CRNA being impaired in the OR, which is a patient safety risk. Second, that Belden's pattern of internal handling rather than referral is consistent with what the OIG flagged as a generic concern in its 2024 healthcare diversion advisory.

I have retained: the reconciliation spreadsheets, the anesthesia record extracts, the dispensing cabinet logs, the peer review minutes, and the general counsel's memorandum. I am willing to identify myself to DEA or to the State Board of Nursing.
